Exam Details

The Texas Journeyman Electrician examination is administered through PSI for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. TDLR states that, starting March 11, 2025, the Journeyman Electrician exam consists of two separate parts: a knowledge portion and a calculations portion. Both portions are multiple choice, and candidates must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%.

The Texas Journeyman Electrician NEC Knowledge Portion includes 59 items, including 3 non-scored items. The time allowed for this portion is 130 minutes, and the minimum passing score is 70%. The content outline includes definitions, theory, plans, electrical services, service equipment, separately derived systems, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, wiring methods, electrical materials, equipment, devices, motors, generators, control devices, disconnecting means, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, photovoltaic systems, and electric vehicle chargers.

The Texas Journeyman Electrician Calculations Portion includes 26 items, including 2 non-scored items. The time allowed for this portion is 110 minutes, and the minimum passing score is 70%. The calculation outline includes electrical theory, service load calculations, electrical service equipment, grounding and bonding, transformers, feeder load calculations, feeder overcurrent protection, branch-circuit calculations, conductor calculations, raceways, air conditioning equipment, refrigeration equipment, heating equipment, appliances, motors, generators, control devices, disconnecting means, mobile homes, park trailers, marinas, and electric vehicle chargers.

The examination fee listed in the PSI bulletin is $78 for both journeyman portions. If a candidate fails one or both portions, the retake examination fee is listed as $78. Time does not roll over from one portion to the next, so candidates should practice pacing separately for NEC knowledge questions and calculation questions.

Texas exam candidates receive approval after TDLR reviews the completed license application and receives the application fee. After approval, candidates may schedule through PSI. TDLR also states that applicants have one year from the date the application was received by TDLR to satisfy all requirements to obtain the license, including passing the examination.

Open Book Test

The Texas electrician examination is an open book test. TDLR and PSI list the National Electrical Code as the allowed reference material. Texas currently lists the National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition for the examination, and candidates are responsible for bringing their own NEC book to the examination site.

PSI’s rules state that any soft-bound edition of the NEC may be used for the examination, but the examination questions are based on the current TDLR-adopted bound edition. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound copies of the NEC are not allowed in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is also not allowed.

Texas allows the candidate’s NEC book to be highlighted, underlined, and contain notes before the examination session. NEC books may be tabbed with permanent index tabs manufactured or provided by the NEC book publisher. Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or mark the NEC during the examination session. Additional paper, whether loose, taped, adhered, stapled, or attached, is not allowed in the examination room.

Because the exam is open book and timed, preparation should include repeated code lookup practice. Students should learn how to move through Article 100 definitions, service rules, feeder requirements, branch-circuit rules, conductor ampacity tables, grounding and bonding provisions, raceway fill, box fill, wiring method articles, equipment rules, special occupancies, and calculation sections. Licensing Steps

  1. Register and gain supervised electrical experience. Texas journeyman candidates must document on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.
  2. Complete at least 7,000 hours before applying to test. TDLR states that 7,000 hours allows an applicant to take the examination before reaching the full 8,000 hours required for licensure.
  3. Obtain experience verification. Candidates must obtain verification from each supervising Master Electrician. The experience must be documented and signed on the required Experience Verification Form.
  4. Submit the journeyman license application. Texas requires the initial Journeyman Electrician license application to be submitted by mail with the non-refundable application fee.
  5. Receive examination approval. After the application is reviewed and verified, TDLR notifies the applicant that they are approved to sit for the licensing exam.
  6. Schedule with PSI. Approved candidates schedule the exam through PSI and follow the testing instructions provided in the candidate information bulletin.
  7. Pass both exam portions. Candidates must pass both the NEC Knowledge Portion and the Calculations Portion with a minimum score of 70% on each portion.
  8. Complete the full licensure requirement. Texas requires the full 8,000 hours of qualifying on-the-job training before the journeyman license is issued.
  9. Renew the license annually. Texas electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and must be renewed annually.

A Texas Journeyman Electrician is licensed to perform electrical work under the general supervision of a Master Electrician. With limited exemptions, anyone who performs electrical work in Texas must be licensed.

TDLR defines electrical work broadly, including labor or material used in installing, maintaining, or extending an electrical wiring system and related appurtenances, apparatus, or equipment used with electrical energy in, on, outside, or attached to a building, residence, structure, property, or premises. Service entrance conductors, as defined by the National Electrical Code, are also included.

To apply for a Texas Journeyman Electrician license, an applicant must have completed at least 7,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas. The 7,000-hour threshold allows the applicant to take the examination before reaching the full 8,000 hours required for licensure. The applicant must obtain signed verification from each supervising Master Electrician, and TDLR may contact individuals to verify the reported experience.

The initial application must be submitted by mail with the required non-refundable application fee. After the application has been received and verified, the applicant receives notification of approval to take the licensing examination. The examination is administered by PSI, and TDLR receives exam results electronically from the testing provider.

Texas electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and must be renewed annually. Licensees should keep their contact information current with TDLR and follow all renewal and continuing education requirements that apply to their license classification.

Exam Details

Texas electrician licensing is overseen by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR), and examinations are delivered through PSI. For the Master Electrician exam, the official Candidate Information Bulletin shows the exam is structured as two separate portions: an NEC Knowledge portion and a Calculations portion. Both portions are multiple choice, and you must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%.

  • NEC Knowledge Portion: 75 items (including 5 non-scored items), 150 minutes, 70% correct to pass
  • Calculations Portion: 33 items (including 3 non-scored items), 170 minutes, 70% correct to pass
  • Exam fee: $78 for both portions (retake fee is also $78 if you fail a portion or both portions)

The content outline published by PSI highlights major areas that show up on the Master Electrician exam. On the NEC Knowledge side, this includes (among other areas) definitions/theory/plan reading, services and grounding/bonding, feeders and branch circuits, wiring methods and materials, equipment and devices, motors and generators, special occupancies/conditions, and renewable energy technologies. On the Calculations side, the outline emphasizes load calculations, grounding/bonding, transformers, feeders, branch circuit calculations and conductors, motors/generators, and related topics.

Open Book Test

The Texas electrician examinations are open book. TDLR’s exam information page states the exam is open book and allows candidates to reference the National Electrical Code (NEC), 2023 Edition. PSI’s bulletin adds important details about what is and is not allowed in the testing room.

  • You must bring your own NEC 2023 to the test site (electronic notepads are provided).
  • Soft-bound NEC editions are permitted.
  • Loose-leaf, spiralbound, or ring-bound copies are not allowed.
  • Your NEC may be highlighted/underlined and may contain notes prior to the exam, but you may not write or mark in it during the examination session.
  • Tabs must be permanent index tabs manufactured/provided by the NEC publisher. Homemade or non-NEC tabs are not allowed.
  • The NEC Handbook is not allowed in the exam room.

Because this is an open-book exam, a major part of passing is not just “knowing code”—it’s knowing where to find it fast, and how to interpret it correctly under time pressure. That’s why practice exams that force you to navigate and apply code rules are such a powerful way to study.

Licensing Steps

Texas Master Electrician licensing begins with meeting TDLR’s experience requirements, submitting your application, receiving eligibility approval, and then scheduling your exam through PSI.

  1. Confirm experience eligibility. TDLR requires Master Electrician applicants to have held a Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years and to document 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.
  2. Collect verification. TDLR requires experience to be documented and signed by supervisors using the required verification method/forms.
  3. Apply by mail with the application fee. TDLR’s Master Electrician application page states that the initial license application must be submitted by mail and includes a non-refundable $45 application fee.
  4. Receive approval to test. After your application is received and verified, TDLR notifies you that you are approved to sit for the licensing exam.
  5. Schedule with PSI. Once eligible, PSI provides scheduling instructions; you can schedule online or by phone.
  6. Pass both exam portions. You must pass the NEC Knowledge portion and the Calculations portion (minimum 70% each).
  7. Maintain your license. TDLR notes electrician licenses are valid for one year and must be renewed annually.

TDLR defines Master Electrician work broadly as installing, maintaining, or extending electrical wiring systems and associated equipment, including service entrance conductors. The state also notes that—aside from certain exemptions—anyone performing electrical work in Texas must be licensed.

For Master Electrician applicants, the key state requirements emphasized by TDLR include:

  • Journeyman held for at least two years (Journeyman Industrial experience may not be used to qualify for the Master Electrician license)
  • 12,000 hours of supervised on-the-job training under a Texas-licensed Master Electrician

Test Information and Study Materials

Knowing the rules of the testing room can save your exam day from unnecessary stress. PSI’s Candidate Information Bulletin outlines common testing policies and what to expect at the computer-based exam site.

  • Two-portion structure: Time does not roll over from one portion to the next, so pacing matters for each portion.

  • Score reporting: Scores are provided immediately after completion (on screen and via a printed score report).

  • Train like the test. Set a timer and take practice exams in realistic conditions—no multitasking, no breaks you won’t have on exam day.
  • Review like it counts. Don’t just check answers—write down what the question was truly testing (definition, exception, table use, calculation pathway, etc.).
  • Build a “miss list.” Track the NEC articles and calculation types you miss most and hit them repeatedly until they become automatic.
  • Practice navigation. Open-book doesn’t mean “easy.” The faster you locate the right section/table, the more time you keep for harder questions.

Master-level exams reward organized preparation. 1 Exam Prep supports your progress by giving you structured practice that mirrors how the test actually feels—question after question that forces you to locate the rule, apply it correctly, and move forward with confidence.

Yes. Texas electrician examinations are open book. You are allowed to reference the National Electrical Code (NEC), 2023 Edition, as long as your book meets the testing room requirements.

The Texas electrician examinations are identified as open book examinations. For the current Texas exam reference rules, candidates are allowed to reference the National Electrical Code edition listed by TDLR and PSI for the examination. Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or mark the NEC during the examination session.

Licensing Steps

A practical Texas licensing path begins by confirming that the Master Electrician license is the correct license for the work and responsibility the candidate intends to perform. TDLR notes that Journeyman Industrial Electrician experience may not be used to qualify for a Master Electrician license. The applicant must also show completion of 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.

The applicant must obtain verification from each Master Electrician who supervised the qualifying work. The experience must be documented and signed by each supervisor on the required Experience Verification Form. If the applicant has held a municipal or regional master electrician license, the applicant may be able to verify on-the-job training for the years that the municipal or regional master license was held.

The initial Texas Master Electrician application is submitted by mail. After the completed application has been received and verified, TDLR notifies the applicant of approval to take the licensing examination.

Texas also regulates electrical contractors separately from individual electricians. A Master Electrician license is an important credential, but contracting activity must also meet the applicable electrical contractor licensing requirements when a person or company performs, offers to perform, or contracts to perform electrical work. The Texas Master Electrician written examination consists of two portions: the NEC Knowledge Portion and the Calculations Portion. Both portions are multiple choice. Candidates must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%. Time from one portion does not roll over into the other portion.

The Texas Master Electrician NEC Knowledge Portion contains 75 items, including 5 non-scored items. Candidates are allowed 150 minutes, and a score of 70% correct is required to pass.

Texas examination rules allow any soft-bound edition of the National Electrical Code to be used for the examination, but exam questions are based on the current TDLR-adopted bound edition. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound copies of the NEC are not allowed in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is not allowed in the examination room.

A candidate’s NEC book may be highlighted, underlined, and may contain notes before the examination session. NEC books may be tabbed only with permanent index tabs manufactured or provided by the NEC book publisher. Open-book testing still requires serious preparation. The exam is not simply about having a code book available. The practice exams help you recognize the subject area being tested. The full final exams help you work through longer exam-style sessions. The flash cards help strengthen recall so you do not have to search for every basic concept during the test.

Licensing Steps

  1. Confirm the Texas Master Electrician license path. Texas Master Electrician licensing is regulated by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.
  2. Hold a qualifying journeyman license. Applicants must have held a Journeyman Electrician license for at least 2 years. Journeyman Industrial Electrician experience may not be used to qualify for a Master Electrician license.
  3. Document required work experience. Applicants must show at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.
  4. Obtain experience verification. Candidates must obtain verification from each Master Electrician who supervised their qualifying work experience, using the required experience verification documentation.
  5. Submit the license application. The initial Texas Master Electrician license application is submitted by mail to TDLR with the required non-refundable application fee.
  6. Receive approval to test. After TDLR receives and verifies the application and experience documentation, the candidate receives notification of approval to take the licensing exam.
  7. Schedule the exam through PSI. After approval, the candidate schedules the Texas Master Electrician examination through PSI.
  8. Prepare with structured study materials. Use the study guide, flash cards, 12 practice exams, 2 full final exams, NEC review, reference-navigation practice, and calculation review to build readiness.
  9. Pass both exam portions. The NEC Knowledge Portion and Calculations Portion must each be passed with a minimum score of 70%.
  10. Maintain the license. Texas electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and must be renewed annually.

This product supports the exam preparation stage. It does not replace the TDLR application process, experience verification, PSI scheduling, license approval, renewal requirements, or state-issued license.

State Requirements

The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation regulates electrician licensing in Texas. With limited exemptions, anyone who performs electrical work in Texas must be licensed. Electrical work includes labor or material used in installing, maintaining, or extending electrical wiring systems and related appurtenances, apparatus, or equipment connected with the use of electrical energy, including service entrance conductors as defined by the National Electrical Code.

A Texas Master Electrician is licensed to install, maintain, or extend electrical wiring systems and related appurtenances, apparatus, or equipment used in connection with electrical energy in, on, outside, or attached to buildings, residences, structures, property, or premises. This license represents an advanced individual credential in the Texas electrical licensing structure.

To apply for a Texas Master Electrician license, the applicant must have held a Journeyman Electrician license for at least 2 years. The applicant must also show completion of at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.

Each supervising Master Electrician must verify the applicant’s experience. If the applicant held a municipal or regional master electrician license, the applicant may verify their own on-the-job training for the years they held that license. TDLR may contact individuals to verify the experience listed in the application materials.

The initial application must be submitted by mail with the required fee. After the completed application has been received and verified, the candidate receives approval to take the licensing examination. Test results are sent electronically to TDLR by the testing provider, so candidates do not need to send their exam results to TDLR.

Texas electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and must be renewed annually. Licensed electricians should follow TDLR renewal, continuing education, supervision, local permit, inspection, and compliance requirements.

Exam Details

The Texas Master Electrician examination is administered by PSI for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. Candidates must first apply through TDLR and receive eligibility approval before scheduling the examination with PSI. After TDLR approves eligibility, the candidate receives instructions for scheduling the exam.

The Texas Master Electrician exam consists of two separate multiple-choice portions: NEC Knowledge and Calculations. Candidates must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%. Time from one portion does not roll over into the next portion, so students should prepare for each portion separately and practice pacing for both sections.

The NEC Knowledge Portion includes 75 items, including 5 non-scored items, and allows 150 minutes. The content outline includes definitions, theory, plans, electrical services, service equipment, separately derived systems, feeders, branch circuit conductors, wiring methods and materials, equipment and devices, motors and generators, control devices and disconnecting means, special occupancies, equipment, conditions, and renewable energy technologies.

The Calculations Portion includes 33 items, including 3 non-scored items, and allows 170 minutes. The calculation outline includes electrical theory, services, service equipment, separately derived systems, load calculations, grounding and bonding, transformers, feeders, branch circuit calculations, conductors, raceways, equipment, appliances, motors, generators, control devices, disconnecting means, special occupancies, and renewable energy technology questions.

The current Texas PSI bulletin lists exam questions as based on the National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition, which is the current TDLR-adopted bound edition for exam purposes. This product is based on the 2026 NEC, making it useful for updated code-cycle study, long-term code development, and reference-navigation practice. Candidates should use the official NEC edition required for the exam they are scheduled to take.

Open Book Test

The Texas Master Electrician exam is an open book test. PSI’s Texas electrician candidate bulletin identifies the National Electrical Code as the allowed examination reference. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own approved NEC book to the examination site.

The Texas exam reference rules are specific. A soft-bound edition of the National Electrical Code may be used for the exam. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound copies of the NEC are not allowed in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is not allowed. Electronic notepads are provided during the exam.

A candidate’s NEC book may be highlighted, underlined, and may contain notes before the examination session. NEC books may be tabbed with permanent index tabs manufactured or provided by the NEC book publisher. Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or mark the NEC book during the examination session. Homemade, DIY, or non-NEC tabs are not allowed. Additional paper, whether loose, taped, adhered, or stapled, is not allowed in the examination room.

This combo includes the National Electrical Code 2026 Paperback with Tabs. It is designed for updated NEC study and code-navigation practice. Because the current Texas exam is based on the 2023 NEC, candidates should use the official code edition and compliant reference setup required by TDLR and PSI for exam day.

Open book testing still requires serious preparation. The NEC is large, detailed, and technical. Students who have not practiced with the code book may lose time searching for basic sections, using the wrong table, overlooking an exception, or missing an article-specific requirement. The strongest candidates understand how to move from a question topic to the correct article, read the code language carefully, check the proper table, and apply the rule accurately.

Licensing Steps

The Texas master electrician licensing path begins with holding a Texas Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years. Texas does not allow journeyman industrial electrician experience to be used to qualify for the Master Electrician license. The master path is intended for electricians who have already progressed through journeyman licensing and gained extensive supervised experience.

The applicant must also document at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas. The applicant must contact and obtain verification from each Master Electrician who supervised the qualifying work. The employment history portion of the application must include the full qualifying experience.

After organizing experience documentation, the applicant submits the Texas Master Electrician license application to TDLR with the required information and fee. TDLR reviews the application and experience. Once the experience has been approved, the candidate becomes eligible to schedule the exam with PSI.

After receiving eligibility approval, the candidate schedules the Texas Master Electrician exam through PSI. The candidate takes both required exam portions and must pass each portion with at least 70%. Score results are provided immediately after completion of the examination, and candidates who do not pass receive a diagnostic report showing strengths and weaknesses by examination type.

After passing the required examination and completing the licensing process, the applicant may be issued the Texas Master Electrician license. Licensees must continue to follow Texas electrical licensing laws, TDLR rules, renewal requirements, continuing education requirements, electrical contractor requirements, local permitting procedures, and the scope of work authorized by the license held.

State Requirements

Texas electrical licensing is administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. Texas requires state-issued electrical licenses for individuals performing non-exempt electrical work. Electrical work must also be performed through a licensed electrical contractor unless an exemption applies.

To qualify for the Texas Master Electrician license, an applicant must have held a Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years, must document 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician, and must pass the master electrician examination. This makes the Texas Master Electrician license an advanced credential built on journeyman licensing and supervised master-level experience.

Texas also issues other electrical license types, including apprentice electrician, residential wireman, journeyman electrician, maintenance electrician, master sign electrician, journeyman sign electrician, journeyman industrial electrician, journeyman lineman, residential appliance installer, and contractor-related licenses. Candidates should pursue the license type that matches the electrical work they intend to perform.

A Texas Master Electrician may perform electrical work, including electrical work performed by journeyman electricians and other electrician license types within the scope allowed by law. However, operating as an electrical contracting business requires the proper contractor license and compliance with TDLR requirements. Individual licensure and business contractor authority are related but separate responsibilities.

Test Information and Study Materials

Texas Master Electrician preparation should begin with the two-part exam structure. Students should study NEC knowledge separately from calculation work because each portion has its own question count, time limit, and passing requirement. A balanced study plan should include code lookup practice, timed calculation drills, missed-answer review, and repeated practice with NEC tables.

The NEC Knowledge portion includes definitions, theory, and plans. Students should review Article 100 definitions, electrical theory fundamentals, plan-reading concepts, symbols, schedules, service layouts, equipment locations, conductor information, panel schedules, and code-compliance details shown in drawings or specifications.

Services, service equipment, and separately derived systems are major study areas. Students should practice service load knowledge, fault current concepts, service disconnect rules, grounding and bonding at services, temporary wiring, transformers, separately derived system grounding, service conductor sizing, and overcurrent protection.

Feeders, branch circuits, and conductors should receive steady attention. Students should review feeder grounding, feeder bonding, feeder overcurrent protection, branch-circuit conductor rules, GFCI and AFCI protection, conductor ampacity, adjustment factors, correction factors, neutral conductor rules, continuous loads, noncontinuous loads, and required outlets.

Wiring methods and materials are central to Texas master electrician preparation. Students should review raceways, cable trays, boxes, enclosures, cabinets, panels, cables, cords, underground wiring, conduit fill, box fill, conductor protection, support rules, wet-location requirements, and Chapter 9 table use.

Electrical equipment and devices should include receptacles, switches, luminaires, appliances, air conditioning equipment, refrigeration equipment, heating equipment, workspace clearance, panelboards, disconnects, and utilization equipment. Motors and generators should include conductor sizing, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, disconnecting means, controllers, generator installation rules, and related calculations.

Special occupancies, equipment, conditions, and renewable energy technologies should also be included in the study schedule. Students should review swimming pools, fountains, RVs, mobile homes, park trailers, marinas, data processing equipment, communications equipment, emergency systems, miscellaneous equipment, photovoltaic systems, and electric vehicle chargers.

Texas journeyman electrician preparation requires more than reading through the code book once. What You Get

  • 2026 Texas Journeyman Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide: A structured study resource for Texas journeyman electrician exam preparation and journeyman-level electrical review.
  • 12 Practice Exams: Multiple practice exam sets designed to help students build repetition, improve pacing, and identify weak subject areas.

Exam Details

Texas electrician licensing is handled through the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. A Texas Journeyman Electrician is licensed to perform electrical work under the general supervision of a Texas licensed Master Electrician. With limited exemptions, anyone who performs electrical work in Texas must hold the proper electrical license for the work being performed.

Texas electrician examinations are administered by PSI after TDLR approves the candidate’s eligibility. After the completed application has been reviewed and the required application fee has been received, the applicant is notified that they are approved to sit for the licensing examination. Candidates then schedule the examination through PSI.

Starting March 11, 2025, the Texas Journeyman Electrician written examination was changed to consist of two separate portions: an NEC Knowledge portion and a Calculations portion. Both portions are multiple choice, and candidates must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%. Time remaining from one portion does not roll over into the next portion.

The Texas Journeyman Electrician NEC Knowledge portion includes 59 items, including 3 non-scored items, with 130 minutes allowed. The Calculations portion includes 26 items, including 2 non-scored items, with 110 minutes allowed. The examination fee is listed as $78 for both portions, and a retake examination fee applies if a candidate fails one portion or both portions.

The NEC Knowledge portion covers Definitions, Theory, and Plans; Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems; Electrical Feeders; Branch Circuits and Conductors; Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials; Electrical Equipment and Devices; Motors and Generators; Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means; Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions; and Renewable Energy Technologies.

The Calculations portion covers Calculations and Theory; Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems; Electrical Feeders; Branch Circuit Calculations and Conductors; Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials; Electrical Equipment and Devices; Motors and Generators; Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means; Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions; and Renewable Energy Technologies. Unless a question specifically notes otherwise, conductors are considered copper.

Open Book Test

The Texas Journeyman Electrician exam is an open-book examination. Candidates are allowed to reference the National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own NEC book to the examination site, and electronic notepads are provided.

Texas has specific exam-room rules for reference materials. Any soft-bound edition of the 2023 National Electrical Code may be used for the examination. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound copies of the NEC are not allowed in the examination room. The NEC book may be highlighted, underlined, and may contain notes before the examination session. NEC books may be tabbed with permanent index tabs manufactured or provided by the NEC book publisher.

Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or mark their NEC book during the examination session. Homemade, DIY, and non-NEC tabs are not allowed. Additional paper, whether loose, taped, adhered, stapled, or otherwise added, is not allowed in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is not allowed in the examination room.

Open book does not mean easy. Candidates still need to understand electrical concepts, recognize how questions are written, locate code sections quickly, apply rules correctly, and manage time across both exam portions. A student who depends only on searching through the NEC for every answer may lose valuable time, especially when moving between knowledge-based questions and calculation-heavy questions.

Open-book preparation should include repeated NEC navigation practice. Students should use the table of contents, index, article structure, definitions, tables, exceptions, notes, and common article locations before test day. Practice exams and final exams help students learn how questions are worded, while flash cards help build recall of formulas, definitions, trade terms, and frequently tested concepts.

Licensing Steps

Texas journeyman electrician licensing begins with supervised electrical work experience. To apply for a Texas Journeyman Electrician license, an applicant must have completed at least 7,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas. Submitting at least 7,000 hours allows the applicant to take the examination before reaching the full 8,000 hours required for licensure.

The applicant must obtain verification from each Master Electrician who supervised the qualifying work. Experience must be documented and signed by each supervisor on the required Experience Verification Form. TDLR may contact individuals to verify the experience submitted with the application.

A typical Texas journeyman path includes registering and working in the electrical trade, gaining supervised on-the-job training under a Texas licensed Master Electrician, documenting qualifying hours, submitting the journeyman electrician license application, paying the required application fee, receiving examination approval, scheduling the PSI exam, passing both portions of the exam, reaching the full 8,000 hours required for licensure, and completing the remaining licensing steps through TDLR.

Applicants must apply by mail for the initial journeyman electrician license application. The Texas Journeyman Electrician license application is submitted with the non-refundable application fee to the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. Electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and must be renewed annually.

This study guide and flash card combo supports the exam-preparation stage of the licensing process. Students can use it while completing supervised on-the-job training, while gathering experience verification, before submitting the application, after receiving examination approval, or during final review before the scheduled PSI exam.

State Requirements

Texas has statewide electrical licensing through the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. Texas licenses electrical workers by classification, including apprentice electricians, journeyman electricians, master electricians, residential wiremen, maintenance electricians, journeyman industrial electricians, journeyman linemen, and sign electricians. This product is focused on the Texas Journeyman Electrician license.

Electrical work in Texas is defined broadly and includes labor or material used in installing, maintaining, or extending an electrical wiring system and the appurtenances, apparatus, or equipment used in connection with electrical energy in, on, outside, or attached to a building, residence, structure, property, or premises. It also includes service entrance conductors as defined by the National Electrical Code.

For the Texas Journeyman Electrician path, candidates must document supervised on-the-job training under a Texas licensed Master Electrician. At least 7,000 hours are required to apply and become eligible to test, while 8,000 hours are required for licensure. Candidates should maintain accurate records of employers, supervising Master Electricians, dates of work, hours completed, work performed, application materials, exam eligibility notices, and licensing documents.

Texas candidates should also prepare with the 2023 National Electrical Code because Texas electrician examinations are referenced to the 2023 NEC. Students should make sure their study routine, practice questions, code book, permanent NEC publisher tabs, and reference navigation are aligned with the current Texas exam requirements.

The bigger task is proving—on paper and under time pressure—that you can interpret the National Electrical Code confidently, choose the right installation requirements, and complete calculations with professional accuracy.

With 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams, it gives you repeated, realistic opportunities to practice how the test actually feels: locate the code section, apply it correctly, and keep moving. Exam Details

The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR) contracts with PSI to deliver electrician examinations. The Texas Master Electrician written exam is organized into two separate portions: NEC Knowledge and Calculations. Each portion is multiple-choice, and you must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%.

  • NEC Knowledge Portion: 75 items (including 5 non-scored items) with 150 minutes to complete
  • Calculations Portion: 33 items (including 3 non-scored items) with 170 minutes to complete
  • Passing requirement: 70% correct to pass each portion
  • Exam fee: $78 for both portions (retake fee is $78 if you fail one portion or both)

The “two-portion” setup matters for your study plan. Even if you feel confident reading code, the calculations portion rewards a different skill set: steady math, correct assumptions, clean steps, and the ability to avoid small errors that cost points. Your prep should train both skills—code navigation and calculation execution—so neither portion becomes a surprise.

The exam content outline highlights major topic areas that commonly appear at the master level. While specific questions vary, your practice should routinely touch the kinds of work you see on real projects: services and equipment, grounding and bonding, feeders and branch circuits, wiring methods, devices and equipment, motors and generators, special occupancies and conditions, and more. Calculations practice often includes load and sizing work that depends on choosing the correct code references and applying them correctly.

Open Book Test

The examinations are open book. The allowed reference is the National Electrical Code (NEC), 2023 Edition, and the Texas Candidate Information Bulletin includes clear rules about what is allowed and what is not allowed in the exam room. The exam also states that effective October 1, 2023, examinations are referenced to the 2023 NEC Code Book.

What is allowed:

  • You are responsible for bringing your own NEC 2023 to the exam site.
  • Soft-bound editions are allowed.
  • Your NEC book may be highlighted, underlined, and/or contain notes prior to the exam session.
  • NEC books may be tabbed with permanent index tabs manufactured and/or provided by the NEC publisher.

What is not allowed:

  • You may not write, highlight, underline, index, or mark your NEC book during the examination session.
  • Homemade/DIY/non-NEC tabs are not permitted.
  • Loose-leaf, spiralbound, or ring-bound copies of the NEC book are not allowed in the examination room.
  • Additional paper (loose, taped, adhered, stapled, etc.) is not allowed in the exam room.
  • The NEC Handbook is not allowed in the examination room.

Open book does not mean easy—it means the exam rewards the electrician who can find the right rule quickly and interpret it accurately. A strong prep strategy focuses on NEC navigation: knowing where definitions live, how chapters are organized, how to use the index effectively, and how to move between articles, tables, and exceptions without losing time.

Licensing Steps

Texas Master Electrician licensing is handled through TDLR. In general, the process includes meeting experience requirements, submitting your application, receiving approval to test, scheduling through PSI, passing the exam portions, and then keeping your license current through renewal.

  1. Meet the experience requirements. TDLR’s Master Electrician requirements include holding a Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years and documenting 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.
  2. Document your experience. Experience must be verified as required by TDLR. Make sure your documentation is complete and matches how the state expects hours and supervision to be reported.
  3. Submit your initial application by mail. TDLR states you must apply by mail for the initial Master Electrician license application, and it includes a non-refundable $45 application fee.
  4. Receive eligibility approval. Once TDLR approves your eligibility, you receive instructions to schedule your exam.
  5. Schedule your exam with PSI. You’ll select a test center, date, and time through PSI’s scheduling process.
  6. Pass both portions of the exam. You must pass NEC Knowledge and Calculations at the required score level.
  7. Renew to keep your license active. TDLR notes electrician licenses are valid for one year and must be renewed annually.

Because the exam is open book and code-referenced, your documentation and eligibility steps are only one side of the process. The other side is building exam performance: timed problem solving, code lookup skills, and consistent accuracy across a wide range of NEC topics.

  • Get comfortable with the index. The index can be faster than flipping chapters if you know how to search terms effectively.
  • Know where tables live. Many time-consuming questions involve tables. Practice locating them quickly and reading them correctly.
  • Reduce “hunt time.” The exam is timed. Every minute you spend searching is a minute you’re not answering questions.

Is the Texas Master Electrician exam open book?

What NEC edition is used for the Texas exams?

The Candidate Information Bulletin states that, effective October 1, 2023, examinations are referenced to the 2023 NEC Code Book, and the allowed reference material is the National Electrical Code (NEC), 2023 Edition.

How is the Texas Master Electrician exam structured?

The Master Electrician written examination consists of two portions: NEC Knowledge and Calculations. Each portion is multiple choice, and you must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%.

How many questions are on the Texas Master Electrician exam?

The NEC Knowledge portion has 75 items (including 5 non-scored items). The Calculations portion has 33 items (including 3 non-scored items).

How much time do I get for each portion?

You have 150 minutes for the NEC Knowledge portion and 170 minutes for the Calculations portion. Time does not roll over from one portion to the next.

What score do I need to pass?

You must pass each portion with a minimum score of 70%.

What NEC book formats are allowed in the exam room?

The Candidate Information Bulletin allows soft-bound NEC editions. It does not allow loose-leaf, spiralbound, or ring-bound copies.

Can I tab and highlight my NEC book?

Is the NEC Handbook allowed in the exam room?

No. The Candidate Information Bulletin states the NEC Handbook is not allowed in the examination room.

Do I have to pass both portions?

Yes. You must pass both portions—NEC Knowledge and Calculations—at the minimum required score.

How should I use the 2 full final exams?

Save them for late in your prep. Take them under timed conditions and use your NEC book exactly as you plan to use it on exam day. Then review results carefully to tighten up your final weak areas.

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians is part of the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. It is intended for individuals who have developed the knowledge and skills needed to perform electrical installation, maintenance, and repair work in accordance with applicable standards and codes.

The examination evaluates journeyman-level electrical knowledge across multiple trade areas. Preparation may involve interpreting electrical plans and specifications, applying basic electrical safety practices, solving theory questions, selecting testing procedures, troubleshooting electrical systems, and using code requirements for different types of installations.

National Electrical Code preparation is a major part of studying for a journeyman electrician examination. Candidates should understand how the NEC is organized and how to use its index, table of contents, articles, definitions, tables, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-references.

Code questions may involve branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding and bonding, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, boxes, raceways, cables, equipment, motors, transformers, special occupancies, special equipment, emergency systems, and communication systems. Candidates should learn how general requirements interact with rules that apply to a particular installation or piece of equipment.

Safety preparation may involve both OSHA regulations and NFPA 70E. Candidates should be able to distinguish between construction-industry requirements, general-industry requirements, and electrical safety-related work practices. Study areas may include hazard recognition, employee protection, personal protective equipment, safe work procedures, electrical shock hazards, arc-flash hazards, and workplace responsibilities.

Electrical theory remains essential even in an open-book exam. A candidate who is unfamiliar with the references may lose significant time searching through the wrong publication or section.

The online exam prep course supports a study method centered on understanding and navigation. Candidates can strengthen their ability to connect electrical questions with the appropriate code article, safety regulation, theory concept, table, formula, or fire alarm requirement.

The goal is to build a repeatable process for finding and confirming information under timed conditions.

Each book serves a different purpose. The National Electrical Code addresses installation requirements. OSHA publications address federal workplace safety standards. A licensing authority may require documented work experience, completion of an apprenticeship program, technical education, employer affidavits, examination approval, application fees, identification documents, or other supporting information.

Open Book Test

The Texas Journeyman Lineman Electrician examination is an open book test.

The approved technical reference is the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026 Edition. Candidates are responsible for bringing an acceptable NEC book to the examination site.

Soft-bound editions of the NEC may be used. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound copies are not permitted in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is also not permitted as the exam-room reference.

The NEC may contain permitted highlighting, underlining, notes prepared before the examination, and compliant permanent NEC index tabs. Candidates may not add new highlighting, notes, underlining, or indexing during the testing session.

Open-book testing rewards familiarity with the reference. Candidates who know where to locate service rules, feeder requirements, equipment provisions, generator articles, grounding requirements, and disconnecting means can use their time more effectively.

The Texas Journeyman Lineman Electrician license is a specialized electrical credential for work on transmission and distribution systems from the original source of electricity to the substation.

Texas recognizes a qualifying pathway involving at least 7,000 hours of training in an apprenticeship program approved by the United States Department of Labor.

The Journeyman Lineman Electrician credential has a limited scope and is different from the Texas Journeyman Electrician license. Candidates should understand the specific work authorized by the license before applying.

Test Information and Study Materials

Definitions and Theory: Six scored items cover NEC terminology and basic electrical theory. Review Article 100 along with voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, conductors, and common electrical relationships.

Electrical Services: Eight scored items involve services, service equipment, and separately derived systems. Review service conductors, service disconnecting means, service ratings, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, and related requirements.

Service Equipment: Study equipment ratings, interrupting ratings, disconnect requirements, grouping, accessibility, identification, and installation practices that apply to service equipment.

Separately Derived Systems: Review transformers, system bonding jumpers, grounding electrode conductors, equipment grounding conductors, and the grounding and bonding requirements that apply to separately derived systems.

Electrical Feeders: Four scored items cover feeders. Study conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounded conductors, grounding and bonding, and feeder installation requirements.

Branch Circuits: Review branch-circuit conductors, overcurrent protection, circuit ratings, and the general NEC provisions that apply to equipment supplied by branch circuits.

Electrical Wiring Methods and Materials: Study the Chapter 3 requirements for raceways, conductors, cables, boxes, enclosures, fittings, supports, physical protection, and wiring methods.

Electrical Equipment and Devices: With 10 scored items, this is the largest exam category. Review equipment installation, equipment ratings, conductor terminations, grounding, accessibility, clearances, overcurrent protection, and general electrical equipment requirements.

Article 110: General Requirements for Electrical Installations are important across many categories. Review equipment listing and labeling, installation and use, conductor terminations, working space, guarding, and interrupting ratings.

Grounding and Bonding: Article 250 can affect services, feeders, equipment, and separately derived systems. Study equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, grounding electrode conductors, grounding electrodes, and fault-current paths.

Overcurrent Protection: Review Article 240 and the relationship between conductor ampacity, overcurrent devices, equipment protection, and circuit requirements.

Conductors: Study conductor ampacity, insulation ratings, temperature limitations, correction factors, adjustment factors, terminal temperature requirements, and conductor identification.

Motors and Generators: Two scored items cover motors and generators. Review conductor requirements, branch-circuit protection, overload protection, disconnects, grounding, and generator-related NEC provisions.

Generators: Become familiar with generator conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, disconnecting means, and other requirements that may apply to generator systems.

Electrical Control Devices: Six scored items are shared between controls and disconnecting means. Review switches, controllers, contactors, disconnect ratings, equipment control, and safe isolation.

Disconnecting Means: Study location, accessibility, ratings, grouping, visibility, lockability, and equipment-specific disconnect requirements.

Transformers: Review transformer conductor protection, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, and separately derived system provisions where applicable.

Equipment Working Space: Review Article 110 working-space requirements, equipment access, clearances, and guarding. Safe access to electrical equipment is a recurring NEC principle.

Code Navigation: Use the 2026 NEC during online exam prep. Practice identifying the main subject of a question before opening the codebook, then move directly to the likely article, table, or section.

Cross-Reference Practice: Many questions may require more than one NEC article. A service question might require Article 230 and Article 250, while a generator question may connect generator rules with grounding, overcurrent protection, or disconnecting requirements.

Timed Practice: Candidates receive 120 minutes for 40 scored items. Practice maintaining a pace of about three minutes per scored question while leaving room for more involved code lookups.

Study by Exam Weight: Give the greatest attention to Electrical Equipment and Devices, Services and Separately Derived Systems, Definitions and Theory, and Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means. These categories represent the largest portions of the examination.

Open Book Test

The Texas Residential Appliance Installer examination is an open book test.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine whether the Residential Appliance Installer license matches your work. The credential is intended for individuals performing electrical work limited to residential appliance installation, including qualifying residential pool-related electrical work.

The individual installer credential and the contractor business license are separate. A Residential Appliance Installation Contractor must employ a licensed Residential Appliance Installer who serves as the installer of record. The installer may also own the contracting business.

Licensing Steps

  1. Hold a Texas Journeyman Electrician license. The Master Electrician credential builds on the Journeyman Electrician license.
  2. Meet the Journeyman license-duration requirement. Applicants must have held the Texas Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years.
  3. Complete the required electrical experience. Applicants must document at least 12,000 hours of qualifying on-the-job training under a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.
  4. Obtain experience verification. Qualifying experience must be documented by the appropriate supervising Master Electrician or Master Electricians.
  5. Prepare the Master Electrician application. The application and supporting documentation are submitted to the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

State Requirements

A Texas Master Electrician is an individually licensed electrical professional. Applicants must have held a Texas Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years and must document at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.

Qualifying experience must be verified as part of the state application process. Journeyman Industrial Electrician experience does not count toward the experience requirement for the Texas Master Electrician credential.

The Texas Master Electrician license and the Texas Electrical Contractor license are not the same credential. The Master Electrician license applies to the individual. The Electrical Contractor license applies to the contracting business.

A Texas electrical contracting business must have a licensed Master Electrician serving as its Master Electrician of Record. The Master Electrician may also own the electrical contracting business.

The business side of electrical contracting can involve more than obtaining the individual Master Electrician credential. A contractor must also establish and maintain the business structure and satisfy the applicable requirements connected with operating as a licensed electrical contracting business.

The current examination uses the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026 Edition.

Exam Details

The NEC may contain permitted highlighting, underlining, notes prepared before the examination, and compliant permanent NEC index tabs. Candidates may not add new markings, notes, highlighting, or indexing during the examination session.

Open-book testing still rewards preparation. Candidates should become familiar with the NEC before test day so they can identify the likely article or section quickly. Repeated reference practice is especially useful for Article 422 appliance requirements and Article 680 pool, spa, and fountain requirements.

NEC Knowledge Portion:

  • Total Items: 75, including 5 non-scored items
  • Time Allowed: 150 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Format: Multiple choice

The NEC Knowledge Portion covers the following subject areas:

  • Definitions, Theory, and Plans: 7 items
  • Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems: 11 items
  • Electrical Feeders: 7 items
  • Branch Circuit Conductors: 11 items
  • Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials: 7 items
  • Electrical Equipment and Devices: 7 items
  • Motors and Generators: 7 items
  • Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: 3 items
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: 7 items
  • Renewable Energy Technologies: 3 items

Calculations Portion:

  • Total Items: 33, including 3 non-scored items
  • Time Allowed: 170 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Format: Multiple choice

The Calculations Portion includes:

  • Calculations and Theory: 2 items
  • Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems: 8 items
  • Electrical Feeders: 3 items
  • Branch Circuit Calculations and Conductors: 4 items
  • Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials: 2 items
  • Electrical Equipment and Devices: 2 items
  • Motors and Generators: 6 items
  • Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: 1 item
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: 1 item
  • Renewable Energy Technologies: 1 item

Time remaining after completion of one examination portion does not transfer to the other portion. Candidates therefore need a separate time-management strategy for code-knowledge questions and calculation questions.

Unless a question specifically states otherwise, conductors are considered copper for examination purposes.

Open Book Test

The Texas Master Electrician examination is an open book test.

The approved technical reference is the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026 Edition. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own compliant NEC book to the testing center.

Any soft-bound edition of the National Electrical Code may be used. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound copies are not permitted in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is not permitted as an examination reference.

The NEC may be highlighted, underlined, and contain notes completed before the examination session. Permanent index tabs manufactured or provided by the NEC publisher are permitted. Homemade, DIY, or non-NEC tabs are not allowed.

Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or otherwise mark the NEC during the examination session. Additional loose, taped, adhered, or stapled paper is prohibited.

Open-book testing still requires strong preparation. Candidates should know which NEC chapter or article is likely to contain the answer before searching. Master-level questions frequently combine several provisions, so simply looking for keywords may not be enough.

Licensing Steps

  1. Hold a Texas Journeyman Electrician license. The Master Electrician pathway builds on the Journeyman Electrician credential.
  2. Maintain the Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years. Texas requires the applicant to have held the Journeyman Electrician license for the required period before applying for Master Electrician licensure.
  3. Complete the required electrical experience. Applicants must document at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.
  4. Obtain experience verification. Each supervising Master Electrician must verify the qualifying experience used for the application.
  5. Submit the Master Electrician license application. The completed application and required documentation are submitted to the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.
  6. Receive examination approval. TDLR reviews the application and notifies approved applicants that they may take the licensing examination.
  7. Schedule through PSI. Eligible candidates schedule the Master Electrician examination with the state testing provider.
  8. Prepare for both examination portions. Study the NEC Knowledge Portion separately from the Calculations Portion while also practicing combined code application.
  9. Use the 2026 NEC during preparation. Become familiar with articles, tables, calculations, definitions, and common cross-references.
  10. Pass both examination portions. A minimum score of 70% is required on each portion.
  11. Complete all remaining licensing requirements. Satisfy the applicable TDLR requirements for issuance of the Master Electrician license.

State Requirements

A Texas Master Electrician is licensed to install, maintain, or extend electrical wiring systems and related apparatus, equipment, and service entrance conductors within the scope established by Texas law.

Applicants must have held a Texas Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years before applying for the Master Electrician license.

Applicants must also document at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.

Journeyman Industrial Electrician experience may not be used to satisfy the experience requirement for the Texas Master Electrician license.

The qualifying experience must be documented and signed by each supervising Master Electrician. TDLR may verify the information submitted with the application.

The Texas Master Electrician license is an individual license. It is distinct from a Texas Electrical Contractor business license. An electrical contracting business must satisfy the separate requirements applicable to Electrical Contractors, including the required Master Electrician of Record structure.

Texas electrician licenses are valid for one year from the date of issuance and are subject to renewal requirements.

The 2026 National Electrical Code became the state electrical code effective September 1, 2026, and the current Master Electrician examination is referenced to this edition.

Test Information and Study Materials

Definitions, Theory, and Plans: Review Article 100 definitions, electrical theory, plan interpretation, voltage, current, resistance, power, and the relationships used in electrical calculations.

Services: Services are an important area on both examination portions. Study service calculations, service conductors, service equipment, disconnecting means, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, available fault current, and separately derived systems.

Feeders: Review feeder ampacity, feeder load calculations, overcurrent protection, grounded conductors, grounding and bonding, and conductor sizing.

Branch Circuits: Branch Circuit Conductors account for 11 items on the NEC Knowledge Portion. Review conductor sizing, continuous loads, overcurrent protection, voltage considerations, grounding, and specialized branch-circuit requirements.

Grounding and Bonding: Article 250 is essential for Master Electrician preparation. Study services, feeders, separately derived systems, grounding electrode conductors, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, and fault-current paths.

Wiring Methods: Review raceways, cables, boxes, enclosures, conductor fill, physical protection, wet locations, underground installations, and Chapter 3 requirements.

Electrical Equipment: Study equipment ratings, receptacles, switches, appliances, HVAC equipment, luminaires, working space, disconnect requirements, and general installation provisions.

Motors and Generators: Motors and generators are especially important in the Calculations Portion, where they account for six items. Review motor full-load currents, conductor sizing, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, controllers, disconnects, generators, and related calculations.

Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: Study controllers, switches, contactors, disconnect ratings, locations, accessibility, grouping, and lockability.

Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: Review hazardous locations, healthcare-related installations, pools, marinas, emergency systems, standby systems, data and communications equipment, and other specialized NEC topics relevant to the examination outline.

Renewable Energy Technologies: Review photovoltaic systems, energy-storage-related code provisions where applicable, and electric vehicle charging equipment.

Service Calculations: These calculations deserve repeated practice. Candidates should understand demand factors, general lighting loads, receptacle loads, appliances, heating and cooling, motors, and other loads used to size services.

Feeder Calculations: Practice feeder load calculations and conductor sizing while applying the appropriate demand factors and NEC requirements.

Motor Calculations: Be comfortable using NEC motor tables rather than relying only on equipment nameplate values when the code requires table values. Practice conductor, overload, short-circuit protection, and feeder calculations involving multiple motors.

Raceway and Box Calculations: Review conductor fill, raceway fill, box fill, pull-box sizing, and conductor volume allowances.

Conductor Ampacity: Practice navigating Article 310 and applying temperature limitations, adjustment factors, correction factors, terminal temperature requirements, and conductor ampacity tables.

Code Navigation: Use the 2026 NEC while completing practice-oriented preparation. Train yourself to recognize the subject of a question before opening the code. This can reduce search time and improve consistency.

Separate Study for Each Portion: Treat NEC Knowledge and Calculations as distinct exam-preparation goals. The Knowledge Portion rewards broad familiarity with code requirements, while the Calculations Portion demands more time per question and stronger numerical application.

Time Management: The NEC Knowledge Portion provides 150 minutes for 75 total items, while the Calculations Portion provides 170 minutes for 33 total items. Candidates should practice under timed conditions so calculations do not consume excessive testing time.

The Texas Plumbing Inspector license is administered by the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners. Licensed Plumbing Inspectors evaluate plumbing work within the jurisdiction of political subdivisions with which they are affiliated. Their role requires the ability to identify compliant and noncompliant plumbing installations, interpret adopted plumbing codes, apply Texas plumbing laws and rules, and evaluate residential and commercial plumbing systems.

The Texas Plumbing Inspector examination is administered through Pearson VUE. The exam evaluates knowledge of plumbing codes, water-heater installations, Texas Plumbing License Law and Board Rules, and major pipe-sizing applications. Examination preparation also involves reviewing illustrations and plumbing installations in order to recognize code violations and correct installation practices.

Texas examination guidance allows candidates to study either the 2018 International Plumbing Code together with the 2018 International Fuel Gas Code or the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code. The Plumbing Inspector examination is not written exclusively around one of these two code systems. This package includes all three books so candidates can build a complete study library and use the code pathway that best fits their preparation approach.

Plumbing inspection requires more than locating isolated code sections. Candidates should understand complete plumbing systems and be able to evaluate how fixtures, drainage, vents, water piping, gas piping, water heaters, traps, cleanouts, backflow protection, materials, joints, supports, and sizing requirements work together. Developing that broader understanding is especially important because the computer-based examination is closed book.

Exam Details

The Texas Plumbing Inspector examination is a state licensing examination administered through Pearson VUE for the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners.

  • Exam: Texas Plumbing Inspector
  • Licensing Agency: Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE
  • Exam Format: Computer based
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Exam Type: Closed book

The TSBPE Plumbing Inspector Examination Review Course identifies the examination content as including 248 multiple-choice questions plus four pipe-sizing exercises. The multiple-choice portion includes:

  • Plumbing Codes in General: 193 questions
  • Water Heater Installation: 30 questions
  • Plumbing License Law and Board Rules: 25 questions

The examination review material also identifies four major sizing exercises:

  • Fuel gas pipe sizing
  • Water pipe sizing
  • Gas-fired appliance vent sizing
  • Drainage system pipe sizing

Many plumbing-code questions involve evaluating full-size, reduced-scale, or illustrated plumbing installations. Candidates should therefore prepare not only to recall code requirements but also to recognize violations in practical system layouts.

Water-heater inspection is a substantial exam topic. Candidates should expect to evaluate installations for issues involving relief valves, discharge piping, combustion air, venting, location, shutoff valves, drain pans, gas connections, and other requirements.

Closed Book Test

The Texas Plumbing Inspector examination is a closed book test. Personal plumbing codes, notes, study guides, papers, and other unauthorized aids are not permitted in the examination room.

The books in this package are intended for study before exam day. Candidates should use them to understand plumbing-code requirements well enough to identify correct and incorrect installations without relying on a personal reference during the test.

A useful preparation method is to study one topic at a time and then practice recalling the rules without the book open. For example, after reviewing water-heater requirements, candidates can work through installation scenarios and identify possible violations from memory before checking the code.

The same approach can be used for drainage, venting, water supply, fuel gas, traps, fixtures, and general installation requirements. Closed-book recall becomes more effective when candidates understand why a rule exists and how it affects an actual plumbing system.

Pipe-sizing exercises should also receive dedicated practice. Candidates should learn the process for evaluating fixture loads, developed lengths, system demand, and the sizing information provided for each type of piping system.

  1. Meet the basic applicant requirements. Applicants must satisfy the eligibility requirements established by the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners.
  2. Meet an approved qualification pathway. Applicants may qualify through an eligible professional license or through the required combination of plumbing-related training and experience.
  3. Complete 500 hours of training and experience when using that pathway. Applicants who do not already hold one of the recognized qualifying licenses may qualify through a combined total of 500 hours of approved plumbing-industry training and experience.
  4. Document qualifying experience. Applicable on-the-job plumbing experience or training in plumbing-code enforcement must be documented through the required Plumbing Inspector employment certification process.
  5. Submit fingerprints. Texas requires fingerprint data for plumbing examination applicants who have not previously completed the requirement with TSBPE.

  7. Receive Authorization to Test. After TSBPE approves the application, Pearson VUE provides examination authorization and scheduling instructions.
  8. Schedule the examination through Pearson VUE. Select an available computer-based testing appointment.
  9. Prepare for code, inspection, law, and sizing topics. Study plumbing systems, water heaters, Texas law and rules, and the four principal sizing applications.

Texas provides several ways to qualify for the Plumbing Inspector examination. An applicant may qualify by holding a current Texas Master Plumber license, Texas Journeyman Plumber license, Texas Professional Engineer license, Texas Architect registration, or a Plumbing Inspector license from another state with substantially equivalent requirements.

Applicants who do not hold one of those qualifying credentials may become eligible by completing a combined total of 500 hours of training and experience in the plumbing industry.

Qualifying training may include approved plumbing-related certifications, training academies, endorsement programs, backflow-prevention training, continuing professional education, plumbing-trade work experience, and supervised plumbing-code enforcement training.

On-the-job work experience in the plumbing trade or an approved similar trade may contribute toward the 500-hour requirement. Documented on-the-job training in plumbing-code enforcement under a licensed Plumbing Inspector may also contribute toward eligibility.

A licensed Texas Plumbing Inspector may inspect plumbing work within the jurisdiction of a political subdivision with which the inspector is affiliated. Affiliation is established through employment by or a contract with the political subdivision to perform plumbing inspections.

A Plumbing Inspector may also perform customer service inspection certification for a public drinking-water system under applicable Texas requirements.

Texas Plumbing Inspectors must avoid financial or advisory interests in plumbing companies when performing inspection duties within their affiliated jurisdiction. The inspector's responsibility is to apply adopted plumbing requirements and Texas plumbing law consistently.

Texas plumbing licenses renew annually. Licensees must satisfy applicable continuing professional education requirements for renewal.
