  • Licensing Agency: Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners
  • Written Testing Provider: Pearson VUE
  • Written Examination Items: 85
  • Written Examination Time: 120 minutes
  • Practical Examination Items: 6
  • Practical Examination Time: 240 minutes
  • Exam Structure: Computer-based written examination plus practical testing when applicable

The written examination evaluates plumbing knowledge across subjects relevant to residential plumbing work. The practical portion requires applicants to demonstrate installation skills using materials furnished for the examination.

Applicants coming from the Plumber's Apprentice level generally proceed to the practical portion after successfully completing the computer-based examination. Pearson VUE communicates written examination results to TSBPE, and successful candidates receive instructions for scheduling the practical component.

The practical examination may be scheduled at designated TSBPE testing locations. Candidates should be prepared to demonstrate actual plumbing installation skills and comply with examination-site clothing and safety requirements.

Closed Book Test

The computer-based Texas plumbing examination is a closed book test. Personal books, dictionaries, papers, scratch paper, study guides, and other reference materials are not permitted in the Pearson VUE examination room.

Because candidates cannot rely on their plumbing books during the written examination, preparation should focus on understanding and retaining the rules rather than simply learning where information appears in a codebook. The code references in this package are study materials used before examination day.

Candidates should repeatedly review common residential plumbing requirements until they can recognize correct installation methods from memory. Study should include drainage slopes, venting principles, fixture requirements, water distribution, water heaters, gas piping, material limitations, cleanouts, traps, sizing, and residential plumbing layouts.

The closed-book format makes practice questions and active recall particularly useful. After reviewing a code topic, candidates should test themselves without looking at the book, then return to the reference to correct mistakes and reinforce the applicable rule.

The practical examination is also skills-based. TSBPE provides the materials needed for that portion, so candidates should arrive prepared to demonstrate installation abilities rather than depend on personal study references.

Licensing Steps

  1. Hold the appropriate Texas registration or qualifying out-of-state license. Applicants generally begin as a Texas Plumber's Apprentice, although qualifying Journeyman or Master Plumbers licensed in another state may also meet an eligibility pathway.
  2. Accumulate qualifying plumbing experience. The standard Tradesman Plumber-Limited pathway requires at least 4,000 hours of experience working in the plumbing trade.
  3. Complete the required examination training. Applicants generally must complete the TSBPE-approved 24-hour training program unless an applicable exemption applies.
  4. Complete fingerprint requirements. Texas requires plumbing examination applicants to have the required fingerprint information on file.
  5. Submit the Tradesman Plumber-Limited examination application. Include the required supporting documentation and employer experience verification.
  6. Receive Authorization to Test. After TSBPE approves the application, the candidate receives testing authorization.
  7. Schedule the computer-based examination. The written examination is scheduled through Pearson VUE.
  8. Pass the written examination. Successful candidates who require the practical component then receive additional scheduling instructions.
  9. Complete the practical examination when required. The practical portion evaluates hands-on plumbing installation abilities.
  10. Complete the license issuance process. After satisfying the examination requirements, complete the remaining TSBPE licensing steps for issuance of the Tradesman Plumber-Limited license.

State Requirements

The standard Texas Tradesman Plumber-Limited examination pathway requires applicants to be registered as a Plumber's Apprentice in Texas and to have at least 4,000 hours of qualifying plumbing experience.

Applicants must also complete a 24-hour TSBPE-approved training program unless they qualify for an exemption. The training program includes continuing professional education, OSHA construction-industry safety training, and instruction involving the International Residential Code and/or Uniform Plumbing Code.

Applicants enrolled in or having completed an apprenticeship program approved by the United States Department of Labor Office of Apprenticeship may qualify under an alternative training pathway. Certain holders of current out-of-state Journeyman or Master Plumber licenses may also be exempt from the 24-hour training requirement.

A Texas Tradesman Plumber-Limited may construct, install, repair, service, or renovate plumbing for one- and two-family dwellings under the supervision of a Responsible Master Plumber.

A licensed Tradesman Plumber-Limited may directly supervise a Plumber's Apprentice on one- and two-family dwelling job sites. When performing plumbing work in a structure other than a one- or two-family dwelling, the Tradesman Plumber-Limited must work under the direct supervision of a licensed Journeyman or Master Plumber who is present at the job site.

Texas plumbing licenses renew annually. Licensees must complete the continuing professional education required by TSBPE to remain eligible for renewal.

Reference Books

  • International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2018
    A residential building-code reference containing plumbing-related provisions for one- and two-family dwellings. It supports study of residential plumbing systems, fixtures, water supply, drainage, venting, water heaters, and related residential construction requirements.
  • International Plumbing Code, 2018
    A comprehensive plumbing-code reference covering fixtures, water distribution, sanitary drainage, indirect waste, vents, traps, interceptors, storm drainage, materials, sizing, testing, and installation requirements.
  • International Fuel Gas Code, 2018
    Covers fuel-gas piping, appliance connections, shutoff valves, pressure testing, combustion air, venting, gas appliances, and related installation and safety requirements. This reference is particularly useful for reviewing gas-fired water heaters and residential fuel-gas systems.
  • Uniform Plumbing Code, 2018
    A plumbing-code reference addressing plumbing fixtures, potable water systems, sanitary drainage, venting, traps, interceptors, water heaters, fuel-gas systems, materials, sizing, and installation practices used in plumbing exam preparation.

Test Information and Study Materials

Water Supply and Distribution: Review residential water-service piping, distribution piping, fixture supply requirements, sizing, pressure, valves, materials, installation, testing, and protection against contamination.

Sanitary Drainage: Study drainage-system layout, drainage fixture units, pipe sizing, slope, fittings, changes in direction, building drains, building sewers, cleanouts, and proper installation methods.

Venting Systems: Understand the purpose of plumbing vents and the methods used to protect trap seals. Review vent sizing, vent connections, individual vents, common vents, wet venting, and termination requirements.

Traps: Review trap requirements, trap seals, prohibited traps, trap-arm limitations, fixture connections, and the relationship between traps and venting systems.

Plumbing Fixtures: Study installation requirements for water closets, lavatories, sinks, bathtubs, showers, laundry fixtures, and other residential plumbing fixtures.

Water Heaters: Water-heater installation is an important study area. Review approved locations, supply valves, temperature and pressure relief valves, discharge piping, drain pans, combustion air, gas shutoff valves, and venting requirements.

Fuel Gas: Use the 2018 International Fuel Gas Code to review gas-pipe sizing, appliance connections, shutoff valves, pressure testing, regulators, sediment traps, combustion air, venting, and safe installation of gas-fired appliances.

Materials: Become familiar with commonly permitted piping materials and their approved applications. Review joining methods, fittings, supports, corrosion protection, and installation requirements.

Plumbing Calculations: Practice code-based sizing involving drainage fixture units, water-supply fixture units, pipe dimensions, developed lengths, and other calculations relevant to residential plumbing.

Residential Plumbing Layout: Review how water, drainage, waste, vent, and gas systems fit together within one- and two-family dwellings. Understanding complete system layouts can help candidates identify installation problems more easily.

Code Terminology: Learn the definitions used by the plumbing codes. Correct interpretation of terms such as building drain, building sewer, fixture drain, vent, trap arm, developed length, and water service is essential when answering technical questions.

Practical Skills: Written knowledge should be reinforced with hands-on practice. Candidates should be comfortable with measuring, cutting, assembling, supporting, and connecting plumbing materials according to accepted installation procedures.

Installation Errors: Practice identifying common code violations involving water heaters, drainage, venting, traps, piping support, connections, valves, and gas appliances. The ability to recognize incorrect installations supports both written and practical preparation.

Closed-Book Recall: Because books and study guides are not permitted in the computer-based examination room, candidates should periodically study without references. Review a topic, close the book, and explain the rule or solve practice questions from memory.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps Texas Tradesman Plumber-Limited candidates organize plumbing-code study around the knowledge and skills needed for residential plumbing work. Preparation can combine technical code review with practice-oriented study and repetition.

Trade-focused review helps candidates strengthen their understanding of water distribution, sanitary drainage, venting, fixtures, traps, water heaters, gas piping, plumbing materials, and residential system layouts.

Because the written examination is closed book, structured review can help candidates move beyond simple code lookup and develop stronger recall of frequently tested plumbing requirements. Repeated practice can help reinforce rules that candidates need to recognize without having the codebook available during the test.

The code references in this package also provide a foundation for understanding why specific installation practices are required. This makes it easier to connect code provisions with practical plumbing work instead of memorizing isolated statements.

Hands-on preparation is important as well. The Texas Tradesman examination includes a practical component for applicable candidates, so study should be supported by real installation experience and familiarity with common plumbing tools, materials, and procedures.

1 Exam Prep supports candidates through organized study guidance, trade-focused review, practice-oriented preparation, code familiarity, and confidence-building study structure. The goal is to provide a clear preparation path without guaranteeing an examination result or license approval.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who licenses Texas Tradesman Plumber-Limited professionals?

The license is administered by the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners.

Who administers the written exam?

The computer-based written examination is administered through Pearson VUE.

Is the Texas Tradesman Plumber-Limited written exam closed book?

Yes. Personal books, study guides, papers, and reference materials are not permitted in the computer-based examination room.

How many questions are on the written exam?

The current computer-based written examination contains 85 items.

How much time is allowed for the written exam?

Candidates receive 120 minutes for the computer-based written examination.

Is there a practical exam?

Yes. Candidates coming from the Plumber's Apprentice level generally complete a practical component after passing the computer-based examination. The current practical component contains six items and allows 240 minutes.

How much plumbing experience is required?

The standard pathway requires at least 4,000 hours of qualifying plumbing experience.

Is training required before applying?

Applicants generally must complete a 24-hour TSBPE-approved training program unless they qualify for an approved exemption or apprenticeship pathway.

What work can a Tradesman Plumber-Limited perform?

A Tradesman Plumber-Limited may construct, install, repair, service, or renovate plumbing for one- and two-family dwellings under the supervision of a Responsible Master Plumber.

Can a Tradesman Plumber-Limited supervise an apprentice?

Yes. A licensed Tradesman Plumber-Limited may directly supervise a Plumber's Apprentice on one- and two-family dwelling job sites.

What happens when working on a building other than a one- or two-family dwelling?

The Tradesman Plumber-Limited must work under the direct supervision of a licensed Journeyman or Master Plumber who is present on the job site.

Which plumbing codes should I study?

Important study references include the 2018 International Plumbing Code and 2018 International Fuel Gas Code or the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code. This package also includes the 2018 International Residential Code for additional residential plumbing study.

What should I focus on during final preparation?

Focus on residential drainage, venting, water distribution, fixtures, traps, water heaters, fuel gas, piping materials, plumbing calculations, installation errors, and hands-on plumbing skills. Because the written exam is closed book, practice recalling important requirements without consulting the code during every question.

Prepare for the Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination with the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026 Edition, the current electrical code reference used for Texas electrician examinations. Texas adopted the 2026 National Electrical Code effective September 1, 2026, making this edition the primary technical reference for candidates pursuing the Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician license through the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

The Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician license is a specialized electrical credential for individuals performing electrical work exclusively at qualifying industrial businesses. The license applies to electrical work at facilities such as chemical plants, petrochemical plants, refineries, natural gas plants, natural gas treating plants, pipelines, and oil and gas exploration and production operations.

This is a limited Texas electrical license. A Journeyman Industrial Electrician may not use this credential to perform general residential or commercial electrical work, and the credential is not equivalent to the Texas Journeyman Electrician license. Experience gained solely under the Journeyman Industrial Electrician license cannot be applied toward the experience requirement for a Texas Master Electrician license.

The licensing examination is administered through PSI for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR). The exam covers electrical definitions, theory, plans, services, feeders, branch circuits, wiring methods, electrical equipment, motors, generators, control devices, disconnecting means, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and electrical safety.

The 2026 NEC is the essential technical reference included in this package. Industrial electrical work requires candidates to move beyond basic code memorization and understand how NEC requirements interact within complex electrical systems. Candidates should be prepared to work with conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, transformers, motors, controllers, disconnects, raceways, hazardous locations, industrial equipment, and electrical safety.

Because the examination is open book, efficient NEC navigation is an important part of preparation. Candidates should practice identifying the subject of a question, moving directly to the applicable article or table, and applying the rule without spending unnecessary time searching through the code.

Exam Details

The Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination is administered by PSI after TDLR has reviewed the applicant's licensing application and qualifying experience.

  • Exam: Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician
  • Licensing Agency: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Scored Items: 60
  • Time for Scored Items: 180 minutes
  • Non-Scored Items: 5
  • Additional Time for Non-Scored Items: 20 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Exam Type: Open book
  • Primary Reference: National Electrical Code, 2026 Edition

The current examination content outline distributes the 60 scored items across the following categories:

  • Definitions, Theory, and Plans: 7 items
  • Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems: 4 items
  • Electrical Feeders: 4 items
  • Branch Circuit Calculations and Conductors: 6 items
  • Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials: 10 items
  • Electrical Equipment and Devices: 6 items
  • Motors and Generators: 7 items
  • Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: 3 items
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: 6 items
  • Electrical Safety: 7 items

Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials is the largest individual category with 10 scored items. Definitions, Theory, and Plans; Motors and Generators; and Electrical Safety each contain seven items. Branch Circuit Calculations and Conductors, Electrical Equipment and Devices, and Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions each account for six items.

Unless an examination question specifically states otherwise, conductors are considered copper.

Open Book Test

The Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination is an open book test.

The current approved technical reference is the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026 Edition. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own acceptable NEC book to the examination site.

Any soft-bound edition of the NEC may be used. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound NEC books are not permitted in the testing room. The NEC Handbook is also not permitted as the examination reference.

The NEC may be highlighted, underlined, and contain notes made before the examination session. Permanent NEC index tabs manufactured or provided by the NEC publisher may be used.

Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or otherwise mark the NEC during the examination. Homemade, do-it-yourself, or non-NEC tabs are not permitted. Additional loose paper or pages attached to the book are also prohibited.

Industrial candidates should practice navigating the NEC sections most relevant to motors, hazardous locations, industrial wiring methods, transformers, services, grounding and bonding, feeders, disconnects, overcurrent protection, and electrical equipment. Knowing where to begin a code search can reduce the amount of time required for each question.

Licensing Steps

  1. Register and work as a licensed electrical apprentice. Qualifying experience must be accumulated while working within the Texas electrical licensing structure.
  2. Work under a Texas-licensed Master Electrician. The required on-the-job training must be performed under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.
  3. Complete 8,000 hours of qualifying on-the-job training. Texas requires Journeyman Industrial Electrician applicants to document the full experience requirement before applying.
  4. Obtain experience verification. Each Master Electrician who supervised qualifying work must complete the required experience-verification documentation.
  5. Submit the Journeyman Industrial Electrician application. The application and supporting documentation are submitted to TDLR for review.
  6. Receive examination authorization. After TDLR verifies the application and qualifying experience, the applicant is approved to test.
  7. Schedule the examination through PSI. Approved candidates use the PSI scheduling process for Texas electrician examinations.
  8. Prepare with the 2026 NEC. Review the official content outline and practice applying NEC requirements to industrial electrical situations.
  9. Take the Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination. Complete the scored and non-scored portions within the allotted testing time.
  10. Earn the required passing score. A score of 70% or better is required.
  11. Complete the licensing process. After satisfying the application, experience, and examination requirements, complete any remaining TDLR steps associated with license issuance.

State Requirements

Texas requires a Journeyman Industrial Electrician applicant to complete 8,000 hours of on-the-job training as a licensed electrical apprentice under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.

Each Master Electrician who supervised qualifying work must verify the applicant's experience. TDLR may review and confirm submitted experience information as part of the licensing process.

The Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician license authorizes electrical work exclusively at a business that operates a chemical plant, petrochemical plant, refinery, natural gas plant, natural gas treating plant, pipeline, or oil and gas exploration and production operation.

The credential is a limited license. Journeyman Industrial Electricians may not perform general residential or commercial electrical work under this credential.

The Journeyman Industrial Electrician license is also not equivalent to the general Texas Journeyman Electrician license. Experience obtained while working as a Journeyman Industrial Electrician does not qualify toward the experience requirement for a Texas Master Electrician license.

The license is valid for one year and must be renewed annually.

Journeyman Industrial Electricians must complete four hours of continuing education during each license cycle before renewal. Required continuing education addresses the National Electrical Code, Texas electrician law, Texas electrician administrative rules, and electrical safety.

Texas adopted the 2026 National Electrical Code as the state electrical code effective September 1, 2026. Current Texas electrician examinations are referenced to the 2026 NEC.

Reference Books

  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026
    The primary technical reference for the Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination. The 2026 NEC covers services, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, raceways, industrial equipment, motors, generators, transformers, controls, disconnecting means, hazardous locations, special occupancies, overcurrent protection, tables, calculations, and other requirements relevant to industrial electrical installations.

Exam Room Approved Books

  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2026
    The 2026 National Electrical Code is the approved technical reference for the current Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination. Candidates must bring a compliant soft-bound copy that meets the testing-center requirements.

The NEC may be highlighted, underlined, and contain permitted notes prepared before the examination. Permanent NEC publisher index tabs may be used. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound versions are not permitted, and the NEC Handbook is not allowed.

Test Information and Study Materials

Definitions, Theory, and Plans: Seven scored items cover NEC terminology, electrical theory, and plan interpretation. Review Article 100 definitions along with voltage, current, resistance, power, transformers, three-phase systems, conductor relationships, and industrial electrical symbols.

Electrical Services and Service Equipment: Review Article 230 requirements for service conductors, service equipment, disconnects, ratings, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, and industrial service arrangements.

Separately Derived Systems: Industrial facilities frequently use transformers and other separately derived systems. Study system bonding jumpers, grounding electrode conductors, grounding electrode connections, and related Article 250 requirements.

Electrical Feeders: Review feeder conductor sizing, ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounded conductors, equipment grounding conductors, load calculations, and industrial distribution systems.

Branch Circuit Calculations and Conductors: Six scored items address branch circuits. Study conductor sizing, continuous and noncontinuous loads, overcurrent protection, ampacity, adjustment factors, correction factors, and branch-circuit requirements.

Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials: With 10 scored items, this is the largest examination category. Review raceways, conduit, cable, conductors, boxes, fittings, cable trays, supports, wet locations, underground installations, and protection from physical damage.

Industrial Raceways: Become familiar with rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, electrical metallic tubing, flexible metal conduit, liquidtight systems, and other wiring methods commonly encountered in industrial environments.

Conductor Ampacity: Study Article 310 tables, conductor insulation, temperature ratings, terminal limitations, adjustment factors, correction factors, parallel conductors, and conductor sizing for industrial loads.

Grounding and Bonding: Article 250 should be a major part of study. Review grounding electrode systems, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, grounding for transformers, service bonding, and effective ground-fault current paths.

Electrical Equipment and Devices: Six scored items cover electrical equipment and devices. Review panelboards, switchboards, transformers, switches, receptacles, overcurrent devices, utilization equipment, and equipment installation requirements.

Motors and Generators: Seven scored items focus on motors and generators. Article 430 is especially important for industrial electricians. Review motor full-load current, conductor sizing, overload protection, branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection, controllers, and disconnects.

Motor Calculations: Practice single-motor and multiple-motor calculations, conductor sizing, overload selection, overcurrent protection, and feeder requirements for groups of motors.

Motor Controllers: Understand controllers, contactors, starters, overload relays, control circuits, and disconnecting means. Industrial systems often require coordinated application of several NEC requirements.

Generators: Review generator conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding, transfer equipment, separately derived system considerations, and installation requirements.

Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: Three scored items cover controls and disconnects. Review ratings, accessibility, location, grouping, lockable disconnects, controllers, and equipment isolation.

Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: Six items address specialized NEC requirements. Industrial candidates should pay particular attention to installations that may involve hazardous or classified locations.

Hazardous Locations: Chemical plants, refineries, natural gas facilities, and oil and gas operations often include areas where flammable gases, vapors, liquids, or combustible materials are present. Review classification concepts and applicable NEC wiring and equipment requirements.

Industrial Equipment: Study equipment installation, working clearances, equipment ratings, overcurrent protection, grounding, disconnects, and environmental considerations.

Electrical Safety: Seven scored items are devoted specifically to electrical safety. Candidates should understand safe work principles involving energized equipment, electrical hazards, equipment isolation, proper protection, grounding, and code-compliant installations.

Code Navigation: Practice moving rapidly between Articles 100, 110, 215, 230, 240, 250, 300, 310, 430, Chapter 5 requirements, and other sections relevant to industrial work.

Timed Practice: Candidates receive 180 minutes for 60 scored items. Develop a steady pace of approximately three minutes per scored question while reserving additional time for calculations or complex code lookups.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician candidates organize study around the subjects included in the state licensing examination. The preparation structure connects practical industrial electrical experience with the requirements of the 2026 NEC.

Trade-focused review can reinforce industrial wiring methods, services, feeders, branch circuits, transformers, motors, generators, controls, disconnecting means, grounding and bonding, hazardous locations, and electrical equipment.

Reference-navigation practice helps candidates become faster and more comfortable using the 2026 NEC. Instead of searching broadly for every question, candidates can learn which articles and tables are most likely to contain the required information.

Motor and industrial-equipment preparation is particularly important because motors, generators, wiring methods, equipment, and safety make up a substantial portion of the examination. Candidates can practice connecting Article 430 requirements with conductor sizing, protection, controls, and disconnects.

Electrical safety review also receives dedicated attention because safety is a separate examination category. Organized preparation can help candidates recognize code requirements that support safe industrial installations and maintenance practices.

The goal is to combine organized study guidance, industrial trade review, NEC navigation, calculation practice, and confidence-building structure. 1 Exam Prep supports exam preparation without guaranteeing a passing score, license approval, or employment outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions

What code edition is used for the Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician exam?

The current Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician examination uses the 2026 National Electrical Code as its approved technical reference.

Is the Texas Journeyman Industrial Electrician exam open book?

Yes. The examination is an open book test.

How many scored questions are on the exam?

The examination contains 60 scored items.

How much time is allowed?

Candidates receive 180 minutes for the scored portion and an additional 20 minutes for five non-scored items.

What score is required to pass?

A score of 70% or better is required to pass.

How much experience is required?

Applicants must document 8,000 hours of on-the-job training as a licensed electrical apprentice under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician.

Can a Journeyman Industrial Electrician perform residential electrical work?

No. The license is limited to qualifying industrial facilities and does not authorize general residential electrical work.

Can a Journeyman Industrial Electrician perform commercial electrical work?

No. Texas identifies the Journeyman Industrial Electrician license as a limited industrial credential that does not authorize general commercial electrical work.

Can industrial electrician experience be used toward a Texas Master Electrician license?

No. Texas does not count Journeyman Industrial Electrician experience toward the experience requirement for a Master Electrician license.

What is the largest exam category?

Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials is the largest category with 10 scored items.

Does the license require continuing education?

Yes. Texas Journeyman Industrial Electricians must complete four hours of approved continuing education during each license cycle before renewal.

What should I focus on during final preparation?

Focus on industrial wiring methods, motors, generators, electrical safety, grounding and bonding, hazardous locations, branch circuits, electrical equipment, services, feeders, disconnecting means, and efficient navigation of the 2026 NEC.

Exam Details

The Texas Journeyman Lineman Electrician examination is administered by PSI after the applicant has been approved to test by TDLR.

  • Licensing Agency: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation

  • Definitions and Theory: 6 items

  • Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials: 2 items

Open Book Test

The Texas Journeyman Lineman Electrician examination is an open book test.

A soft-bound edition of the NEC may be used. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound NEC copies are not permitted in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is also not permitted as the examination reference.

Licensing Steps

  4. Document qualifying experience. Experience must be verified and signed by the appropriate supervising electrician.
  5. Submit the Journeyman Lineman license application. The application and required supporting documentation are submitted to TDLR for review.

  7. Schedule the exam with PSI. Approved candidates follow the PSI scheduling instructions for the Texas Journeyman Lineman Electrician examination.
  8. Prepare with the 2026 NEC. Study the official examination categories and practice efficient navigation of the current code.
  9. Take the licensing examination. Complete the scored and non-scored items within the allotted testing time.
  10. Achieve the required passing score. Candidates must score at least 70%.
  11. Complete the licensing process. After satisfying the application, experience, and examination requirements, complete any remaining TDLR requirements for license issuance.

State Requirements

A Texas Journeyman Lineman is licensed to engage in electrical work involving the maintenance and operation of equipment associated with the transmission and distribution of electricity from its original source to a substation for further distribution.

The Texas Master Electrician examination is administered through PSI for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR). The examination is divided into two separate portions: an NEC Knowledge Portion and a Calculations Portion. Both portions are multiple choice, and candidates must earn at least 70% on each portion.

The Texas Master Electrician credential is also closely connected to the Texas Electrical Contractor license. Texas requires an Electrical Contractor business to employ a licensed Master Electrician as its Master Electrician of Record, although the business owner may personally hold the Master Electrician license and assign that license to the company. For candidates planning to operate an electrical contracting business, earning the Master Electrician license can therefore be an important step toward meeting the contractor-license structure established by TDLR.

The 2026 National Electrical Code is the central technical reference for this package. Candidates should be prepared to navigate services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor sizing, wiring methods, grounding and bonding, electrical equipment, motors, generators, controls, disconnects, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, renewable-energy systems, and advanced electrical calculations.

Master-level preparation requires more than memorizing code sections. Candidates need to understand how NEC rules interact and how to apply tables, exceptions, adjustment factors, demand factors, equipment requirements, and calculation procedures. Efficient reference navigation is especially important because the examination is open book but subject to strict time limits.

Exam Details

The Texas Master Electrician examination currently consists of two separately timed portions. Both portions must be passed with a minimum score of 70%.

NEC Knowledge Portion:

  • Total Items: 75, including 5 non-scored items
  • Time Allowed: 150 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%
  • Format: Multiple choice

The NEC Knowledge Portion is divided into the following subject areas:

  • Definitions, Theory, and Plans: 7 items
  • Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems: 11 items
  • Electrical Feeders: 7 items
  • Branch Circuit Conductors: 11 items
  • Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials: 7 items
  • Electrical Equipment and Devices: 7 items
  • Motors and Generators: 7 items
  • Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: 3 items
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: 7 items
  • Renewable Energy Technologies: 3 items

Calculations Portion:

  • Total Items: 33, including 3 non-scored items
  • Time Allowed: 170 minutes

The Calculations Portion includes:

  • Calculations and Theory: 2 items

  • Electrical Equipment and Devices: 2 items
  • Motors and Generators: 6 items
  • Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means: 1 item
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: 1 item
  • Renewable Energy Technologies: 1 item

Unless a question specifically states otherwise, examination conductors are treated as copper.

Open Book Test

The Texas Master Electrician examination is an open book test.

The current TDLR examination information allows candidates to reference the National Electrical Code, 2026 Edition. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own NEC book to the examination center.

A soft-bound edition of the National Electrical Code may be used. Loose-leaf, spiral-bound, and ring-bound NEC copies are not permitted in the examination room. The NEC Handbook is also not permitted as the examination reference.

The NEC book may be highlighted and underlined before the examination and may contain notes made before the testing session. Permanent index tabs manufactured or provided for use with the NEC book may be used under the examination rules.

Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, index, or otherwise mark the NEC during the examination session. Homemade tabs, non-NEC tabs, temporary removable markers, and additional loose paper are not permitted.

Open-book preparation should therefore include organizing the NEC before exam day and practicing navigation. Candidates should know where to locate frequently tested subjects instead of relying on the index for every question.

Licensing Steps

  1. Hold a Texas Journeyman Electrician license for at least two years. Texas requires Master Electrician applicants to have held the Journeyman Electrician license for the required period.
  2. Complete the required on-the-job training. Applicants must document at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.
  3. Obtain experience verification. Qualifying experience must be documented through the appropriate TDLR experience-verification process.
  4. Submit the Master Electrician application. The application is reviewed by TDLR before examination eligibility is granted.
  5. Receive examination authorization. Once approved, candidates receive instructions for scheduling the Master Electrician examination through PSI.
  6. Prepare with the 2026 NEC. Review both the NEC Knowledge and Calculations content outlines and practice using the current code edition.

  8. Take the Calculations Portion. Complete the 33-item portion within 170 minutes.

The applicant must also document at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Texas-licensed Master Electrician. TDLR requires qualifying experience to be properly verified.

A Texas Master Electrician is authorized to install, maintain, or extend electrical wiring systems and the equipment associated with the use of electrical energy, including service-entrance conductors, within the scope established by Texas law.

The Master Electrician license is an individual credential. The Electrical Contractor license is a separate business credential. To obtain or maintain an Electrical Contractor license, the business must employ a licensed Master Electrician as the Master Electrician of Record, or the business owner may serve in that role if the owner personally holds the Master Electrician license.

A Master Electrician generally may be assigned to one Electrical Contractor unless the Master Electrician owns more than 50% of the electrical contracting business under the applicable Texas rules.

Texas adopted the 2026 National Electrical Code as the state electrical code effective September 1, 2026. The adoption includes a limited Texas exception relating to certain ground-fault circuit-interrupter requirements for outdoor outlets serving HVAC equipment.

Test Information and Study Materials

Separately Derived Systems: Review transformers, grounding and bonding of separately derived systems, system bonding jumpers, grounding electrode conductors, and related Article 250 requirements.

Feeders: Study Article 215 requirements, feeder conductor sizing, ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, neutral calculations, and feeder demand calculations.

Branch Circuits: Branch-circuit conductors are one of the largest NEC Knowledge categories. Review Article 210, conductor sizing, loads, required circuits, receptacle requirements, GFCI protection, AFCI protection, and branch-circuit ratings.

Load Calculations: Master-level candidates should be comfortable with Article 220 calculations involving dwelling units, commercial loads, lighting, receptacles, appliances, ranges, dryers, motors, heating, cooling, demand factors, and service or feeder sizing.

Grounding and Bonding: Study Article 250 in depth. Review grounding electrode systems, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, services, separately derived systems, feeders, grounding electrode conductor sizing, and fault-current paths.

Wiring Methods: Review Chapter 3 wiring methods, conductor installation, raceways, cables, boxes, conduit bodies, supports, wet locations, underground installations, physical protection, and conductor fill.

Conductor Ampacity: Practice using Article 310 tables, temperature limitations, conductor insulation ratings, adjustment factors, correction factors, parallel conductors, and equipment termination requirements.

Review Article 430 motor full-load currents, conductor sizing, overload protection, branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection, controllers, disconnecting means, and multiple-motor calculations.

Controls and Disconnects: Review control equipment, disconnect ratings, location requirements, accessibility, grouped disconnects, and equipment-specific disconnecting requirements.

Special Occupancies: Prepare for hazardous locations, health-care facilities, assembly occupancies, commercial garages, marinas, agricultural buildings, and other Chapter 5 installations.

Special Equipment: Review elevators, signs, cranes, welders, generators, electric vehicle power-transfer systems, photovoltaic systems, energy storage systems, pools, fountains, and other Chapter 6 equipment.

Special Conditions: Study emergency systems, legally required standby systems, optional standby systems, energy storage, interconnected power-production sources, and other Chapter 7 requirements.

Renewable Energy Technologies: Review photovoltaic systems, energy storage, interconnected sources, and related NEC requirements. Renewable-energy topics appear in both examination portions.

Timed Practice: The NEC Knowledge Portion allows 150 minutes for 75 items, while the Calculations Portion allows 170 minutes for 33 items. Practice code lookups and calculations separately because the allotted time from one portion does not carry over to the other.

Prepare for the Texas Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Certified Technician examination with a comprehensive collection of Texas licensing references, current mechanical and fuel-gas codes, HVACR technical material, safety information, and air-distribution resources. This book package supports candidates preparing for the Texas ACR Certified Technician Examination administered for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

Texas distinguishes the Certified Technician designation from an Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor license. A Certified Technician works under the supervision of a licensed Texas Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor and may assist with air-conditioning and refrigeration maintenance and repair work within that supervised employment structure. The Certified Technician designation is a voluntary qualification above the Registered Technician level and requires applicants to satisfy TDLR eligibility requirements and pass the Certified Technician examination.

This package brings together references covering Texas Air Conditioning and Refrigeration law and rules, occupational safety, mechanical systems, fuel-gas installations, refrigeration principles, HVACR equipment, troubleshooting, controls, service, and air distribution. The combination supports both examination preparation and broader understanding of the regulatory and technical responsibilities encountered in Texas HVACR work.

Texas updated its adopted mechanical and fuel-gas codes effective September 1, 2026. Current preparation should therefore account for the 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code, 2024 International Mechanical Code, and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code. These editions are included in this package along with Texas law and rules and the 22nd edition of Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning.

Effective exam preparation requires more than reading each book from beginning to end. Candidates should understand which reference addresses a particular subject and become comfortable locating information efficiently. Mechanical installation questions may direct candidates to the IMC or UMC, gas-related subjects to the IFGC, licensing requirements to Texas law and administrative rules, and technical refrigeration or troubleshooting concepts to Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning.

Exam Details

Applicants seeking Texas Certified Technician status take the TX ACR Certified Technician Examination. The examination is administered through PSI for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

  • Exam: TX ACR Certified Technician Examination
  • Licensing Agency: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Credential: Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Certified Technician
  • Minimum Applicant Age: 18 years old

Candidates must first apply to TDLR and demonstrate that they meet the qualification requirements for Certified Technician status. After TDLR verifies eligibility, the applicant receives examination eligibility information and instructions for registering and scheduling the examination through PSI.

The Certified Technician exam is separate from the contractor endorsement examinations. Texas contractor applicants may take Commercial Refrigeration Class A, Environmental Air Class A, Commercial Refrigeration Class B, or Environmental Air Class B examinations depending on the license class and endorsement selected. Certified Technician applicants instead take the dedicated TX ACR Certified Technician Examination.

Because the technician exam is designed for individuals working directly with air-conditioning and refrigeration systems, candidates should prepare broadly across HVACR fundamentals, equipment operation, controls, refrigeration, mechanical-system requirements, gas-related concepts, safety, and Texas regulatory requirements.

Open Book Test

The Texas ACR Certified Technician examination uses approved reference materials identified for the examination by TDLR and PSI. Candidates should prepare their permitted books before test day and follow the current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin for examination-room material rules.

Reference preparation is an important part of studying. Knowing where to find definitions, equipment requirements, mechanical-system provisions, fuel-gas requirements, refrigeration concepts, safety information, and Texas licensing rules can reduce time spent searching during testing.

Candidates should become familiar with the structure of the 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code, 2024 International Mechanical Code, and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code. Each code serves a different purpose, and recognizing which book applies to a question can make reference navigation more efficient.

Technical preparation should also include Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning, 22nd Edition. This reference supports understanding of refrigeration cycles, compressors, evaporators, condensers, metering devices, refrigerant behavior, electrical systems, controls, heating and cooling equipment, service procedures, and troubleshooting.

The included Ductulator provides another useful study resource for airflow and duct-system concepts. Candidates can use it to strengthen familiarity with duct dimensions, airflow quantities, friction rate, and velocity relationships.

Licensing Steps

The Texas Certified Technician designation is administered by TDLR. Applicants must meet an approved qualification pathway before becoming eligible to take the examination.

  1. Meet the minimum age requirement. Applicants must be at least 18 years old.
  2. Qualify through practical experience or approved training. Texas provides an experience pathway and an approved certification-training pathway.
  3. Use the practical-experience pathway when applicable. Applicants may qualify by documenting at least 24 months of air-conditioning and refrigeration-related work under the supervision of a licensed Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor.
  4. Use approved training when applicable. Applicants may also qualify by completing a department-approved certification program consisting of 2,000 hours of combined instruction and practical experience.
  5. Submit the Certified Technician application. Applicants must provide the required application and qualifying documentation to TDLR.
  6. Receive examination eligibility. TDLR reviews the application and verifies that the applicant satisfies the eligibility requirements.
  7. Register with PSI. After approval, candidates receive instructions for scheduling the TX ACR Certified Technician Examination.
  8. Prepare with the applicable reference materials. Review Texas law, mechanical codes, fuel-gas requirements, HVACR technical principles, service procedures, controls, and safety.
  9. Take and pass the Certified Technician examination. Complete the PSI examination within the application eligibility period.
  10. Maintain the Certified Technician designation. Certified Technicians must continue to work within the Texas supervision and credential requirements that apply to technicians.

State Requirements

Texas defines Certified Technician status as a technician qualification rather than a contractor license. A person holding the designation may call themselves a Certified Technician, but the credential does not independently authorize the technician to operate as an Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor.

Certified Technicians performing regulated air-conditioning and refrigeration work must work under the supervision of a licensed Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor. Technicians may not independently advertise air-conditioning and refrigeration contracting services under the technician credential.

An applicant can qualify through practical experience by documenting at least 24 months of air-conditioning and refrigeration-related work performed under the supervision of a licensed Texas Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor.

Military HVACR experience may be combined with or used toward the practical-experience requirement when properly documented according to TDLR requirements.

Texas also permits qualification through a TDLR-approved Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Certification Training Program. The approved program must consist of 2,000 hours of combined instruction and practical experience. Applicants using this pathway must meet the applicable timing and documentation requirements associated with completion of the program.

Certified Technician status can also become part of a future contractor-license pathway. A person who has held the Certified Technician designation for the preceding 12 months and has accumulated at least 36 months of qualifying practical air-conditioning and refrigeration experience during the preceding 48 months may qualify to apply for a Texas Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractor license, subject to all applicable contractor requirements.

This makes the Certified Technician credential useful both as a professional technician designation and as a potential step toward contractor-level licensing for individuals who continue to gain qualifying experience.

Test Information and Study Materials

Refrigeration Principles: Review the basic refrigeration cycle and the relationship between compression, condensation, expansion, and evaporation. Understand sensible heat, latent heat, saturation, pressure-temperature relationships, superheat, and subcooling.

Compressors: Study common compressor types, operation, electrical requirements, lubrication, capacity, failure conditions, and troubleshooting. The compressor is a central component of both air-conditioning and refrigeration systems.

Evaporators and Condensers: Understand heat absorption at the evaporator and heat rejection at the condenser. Review airflow, temperature differences, refrigerant conditions, coil cleanliness, and common performance problems.

Metering Devices: Review thermostatic expansion valves, fixed metering devices, and other methods used to regulate refrigerant entering an evaporator. Understand how metering-device operation affects superheat and overall system performance.

Electrical Systems and Controls: HVACR technicians frequently work with thermostats, relays, contactors, capacitors, motors, transformers, pressure switches, control boards, and safety controls. Review electrical troubleshooting and common control-circuit operation.

Air Distribution: Study airflow, supply and return systems, duct sizing, static pressure, velocity, friction loss, registers, grilles, filters, and common airflow problems. The Ductulator can support practical study in this area.

Mechanical Codes: Use the 2024 IMC and UMC to review mechanical-equipment installation, access, clearances, ventilation, duct systems, exhaust, refrigeration systems, condensate disposal, combustion air, and equipment safety.

Fuel Gas: Use the 2024 IFGC to review gas piping, pressure testing, shutoff valves, regulators, appliance connections, combustion air, vent connectors, venting systems, and fuel-burning appliance requirements.

Service and Troubleshooting: Practice diagnosing symptoms such as inadequate cooling, high or low system pressures, improper superheat or subcooling, airflow restrictions, compressor problems, electrical faults, and control failures.

Refrigerant Handling: Review safe procedures involving system charging, recovery, evacuation, leak detection, cylinders, hoses, gauges, and pressure hazards. Technicians should understand how refrigerant conditions affect both system performance and servicing procedures.

Heating Equipment: Study gas-fired heating equipment, electric heating equipment, heat pumps, controls, combustion considerations, and common service issues encountered in environmental air systems.

Commercial Refrigeration: Review coolers, freezers, condensing units, evaporators, defrost systems, temperature controls, refrigeration piping, and other commercial applications that may be encountered by an HVACR technician.

Safety: Use OSHA material and technical references to strengthen awareness of workplace hazards, electrical safety, pressurized systems, hot surfaces, moving equipment, refrigerant handling, and proper work practices.

Texas Law and Rules: Review the difference between Registered Technician, Certified Technician, and Contractor credentials. Understand supervision requirements and the limitations placed on technicians working under a contractor.

Reference Navigation: Practice identifying the type of question before opening a reference. A gas-appliance question may require the IFGC, a mechanical installation question may require the IMC or UMC, a technician-rule question may require Chapter 75, and a refrigeration-theory question may lead to Modern Refrigeration and Air Conditioning.

The Commercial Refrigeration endorsement applies to the use of mechanical or absorption equipment to control temperature or humidity in order to satisfy the intended use of a particular space. Process Cooling or Heating relates to control of temperature, humidity, or cleanliness for production requirements or proper operation of equipment.

The Class B license differs from Class A primarily in its capacity limitation. A Class A license permits work on equipment of any size within the authorized endorsement, while Class B remains subject to the applicable cooling and heating capacity limits.

The standard Texas experience pathway requires at least 48 months of practical air-conditioning and refrigeration experience during the preceding 72 months. Applicants must document qualifying experience according to TDLR requirements.

The Texas Journeyman Electrician examination is administered by PSI for the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. Applicants must first submit the required license application and experience documentation to TDLR and receive approval before scheduling the examination.

The current Texas Journeyman Electrician examination contains 80 scored questions. Candidates are allowed 240 minutes, or four hours, for the scored portion. The examination also includes five non-scored questions with an additional 20 minutes. A score of at least 70 percent is required to pass.

The examination content is divided among several major technical areas. Definitions, Calculations, Theory, and Plans account for six scored questions. Candidates should understand electrical terminology, fundamental theory, mathematical relationships, code definitions, and basic plan interpretation.

Electrical Services, Service Equipment, and Separately Derived Systems account for nine scored questions. Preparation should include service calculations, service conductors, service equipment, disconnecting means, transformers, grounding, bonding, and separately derived systems.

Electrical Feeders account for three scored questions, while Branch Circuit Calculations and Conductors account for 15. Candidates should be comfortable with feeder loads, branch-circuit requirements, conductor ampacity, adjustment and correction factors, overcurrent protection, required circuits, GFCI protection, AFCI protection, and conductor sizing.

Electrical Wiring Methods and Electrical Materials represent the largest examination category with 18 scored questions. This makes raceways, cables, boxes, fittings, cabinets, enclosures, support requirements, underground installations, conductor installation, permitted wiring methods, and physical protection important areas of study.

Electrical Equipment and Devices account for 10 scored questions. Preparation can include receptacles, switches, luminaires, appliances, utilization equipment, heating and cooling equipment, panelboards, disconnecting means, and other equipment regulated by the NEC.

Motors and Generators account for five scored questions. Candidates should understand motor conductors, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, controllers, disconnects, generators, and the calculations associated with these installations.

Electrical Control Devices and Disconnecting Means account for three scored questions. Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions account for nine, while Renewable Energy Technologies account for two.

Unless a test question specifically indicates otherwise, the current Texas examination instructs candidates to consider conductors as copper. This is an important testing convention when working through conductor-sizing and calculation questions.

FAQ: Is the Texas Master Electrician exam open book?

Yes. The Texas Master Electrician exam is open book. Candidates are allowed to use the National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition, as long as the NEC book meets PSI and TDLR examination rules.

FAQ: How many portions are on the Texas Master Electrician exam?

The Texas Master Electrician written exam has two portions: NEC Knowledge and Calculations. Each portion is multiple choice, and each portion must be passed with a minimum score of 70%.

FAQ: How many questions are on the Texas Master Electrician exam?

The NEC Knowledge portion includes 75 items, including 5 non-scored items. The Calculations portion includes 33 items, including 3 non-scored items.

FAQ: What experience is required for a Texas Master Electrician license?

Texas requires an applicant to have held a Journeyman Electrician license for at least 2 years and document 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under the supervision of a Master Electrician licensed in Texas.
